posts.content:
Before the Hormuz conflict, Dubai handled the majority of Middle East air cargo. That share dropped when the conflict started and hasn't come back in any phase since, including the ceasefire.

Dubai's volume is actually up about 11% from its pre-conflict baseline. Istanbul and Frankfurt have grown faster. Both now handle more daily cargo than Dubai. Istanbul gained ground in every single phase of the crisis without a pause. Frankfurt grew too, though rising dwell times there point to congestion rather than clean capacity absorption.

Transit times are above pre-conflict baseline in every phase as well.

For supply chain leaders routing goods through the Gulf, this may not be a temporary workaround. The data suggests it's how air cargo routes now.

Full data in the Hormuz Supply Chain Insights report. Link in comments.

posts.content:
The supply chain headlines have been all about ocean this year: Hormuz, Red Sea, tariffs.

But there's a lot happening in North American truckload that isn't getting the same attention.

Ben Steffes breaks it down:
→ Tender rejection rate hit 17% and is sitting around 15.5% — still one in six contracted loads getting rejected
→ Cash freight index down 4% year-over-year, and declining month-over-month
→ 8,000+ carrier authorities revoked over two years; H1 2026 saw a 31% spike in DOT authority revocations
→ For the first time in 45 months, spot rates exceeded contract rates in June 2026

Carriers have the upper hand for the first time in nearly four years. Routing guides are eroding. Primary carriers are chasing spot market dollars.

For shippers and transportation teams: this is what a freight cycle inflection point looks like. 👇
